newsitem.title: USA: Renewable fuels to blunt 'oil weapon'-US official.
newsitem.headline: Renewable fuels to blunt 'oil weapon'-US official.

text.p: The United States can "blunt the oil weapon" -- the threat of a cut-off of foreign oil -- by development of home-grown fuels like ethanol, an Energy Department official said Wednesday.
"We can blunt the oil weapon entirely," Principal Deputy Assistant Energy Secretary Joseph Romm said, if renewable fuels were harnessed and took a larger share of U.S. energy sources.
Romm and Keith Collins, chief economist at the Agriculture Department, foresaw rising ethanol output. Romm also pointed to the potential of biomass crops to reduce ethanol prices.

Former CIA director James Woolsey and Romm said development of renewable fuels would lessen U.S. reliance on oil imports. Woolsey said political instability made the Middle East an uncertain supplier.

Renewable fuels, such as ethanol, could furnish 10-20 percent of U.S. oil needs, Romm said, citing research that might lower the cost of producing ethanol to 70 cents per gallon by 2010. That would make ethanol competitive, without subsidies, with gasoline at $25 per barrel of oil.
Romm said large scale use of biomass fuels in vehicles would require crops "grown specifically for energy purposes."
Some types of grasses and fast-growing trees were being tested as possible biomass sources.
In the near term, Collins said ethanol production, crimped by high corn prices, should pick up volume this month as the new crop comes onto the market.
"Over time, we believe ethanol production will regain the ground lost this past year and expand beyond the peak production year of 1995," he said.
USDA projects 650 million bushels of corn could be used for ethanol in 2000. One bushel yields 2.5 gallons. In 1995, 1.3 billion gallons were produced.
